questions.q: What makes a reward "genuinely verifiable" for this capstone, as opposed to merely plausible to check?
options: It is scored by a large, powerful judge model
It is computed by a cheap, deterministic checker against ground truth — like exact answer matching or passing unit tests — rather than a learned or fuzzy judgment
It is based on how long the response is
It is whatever a human annotator feels is best
questions.explain: A verifiable reward comes from a fixed program checking against ground truth (an exact math answer, or passing unit tests), not from a trained or subjective judgment call.

questions.q: Why is a verifiable-reward checker less vulnerable to the overoptimization problem described in Chapter 6's reward modeling lessons?
options: It isn't actually less vulnerable; the same risk applies equally
Because it's a fixed, deterministic program rather than a trained model, so it can't drift or be exploited the way an optimized learned reward model can
Because verifiable tasks never use PPO
Because it only works on very large models
questions.explain: A learned reward model can be overoptimized because the policy can find proxy-exploiting outputs; a fixed verifier program has no learned parameters to exploit in that way.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend starting from an already instruction-tuned checkpoint rather than a raw base model?
options: Raw base models cannot run on a GPU
Instruction tuning is required by the TRL library and cannot be skipped
Starting from an instruction-tuned model avoids spending the capstone's limited training time on relearning basic prompt-following and formatting before RL can focus on the task itself
Base models are always larger than instruction-tuned ones
questions.explain: An instruction-tuned starting point already follows the prompt format, so PPO training time is spent improving task performance rather than teaching basic formatting from scratch.

questions.q: Why must the held-out evaluation set be set aside before PPO training begins, not selected afterward?
options: It doesn't matter when it's selected, as long as it's the right size
Because held-out data must come from a different dataset entirely
So that none of its examples could have influenced training, which is necessary for lesson 69's evaluation to honestly measure improvement over the baseline
Because PPO requires the held-out set as an input to its loss function
questions.explain: An evaluation set is only meaningful if it was never seen during training; carving it out upfront guarantees that later evaluation isn't contaminated by training exposure.

questions.q: Which of the following would disqualify a task from being a good capstone choice, per this lesson?
options: The task has a ground-truth numeric answer that can be checked exactly
The task can be checked by running generated code against unit tests
The task's quality can only be judged by whether a response "sounds good," with no mechanical way to check it
The task dataset is available on the Hugging Face Hub
questions.explain: A task whose only check is a fuzzy, subjective judgment has no verifiable reward — that's exactly the gap learned reward models exist to fill, and it's unsuitable for this capstone's verifiable-reward approach.
